questions.stem: In 2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl, the chlorine is

options.text: The oxidising agent, reduced from 0 to -1 as each atom gains an electron
options.explanation: Chlorine takes the electrons sodium loses, which is reduction and hence oxidising behaviour.

options.text: The reducing agent, oxidised from 0 to -1
options.explanation: Gaining electrons is reduction; the agent that causes oxidation is itself reduced.

options.text: Oxidised, losing electrons to sodium
options.explanation: Electron flow runs from sodium to chlorine, not the reverse.

options.text: A catalyst that speeds the metal's oxidation
options.explanation: Chlorine is consumed into the salt, so it is a reactant.

questions.stem: Calcium reacting with bromine forms CaBr2 because

options.text: Two bromine atoms share their electrons with calcium covalently
options.explanation: The product is ionic, not covalent.

options.text: Each calcium atom loses two electrons, needing two bromine atoms to accept one each
options.explanation: Ca -> Ca2+ + 2e- pairs with Br2 + 2e- -> 2Br-, giving the 1:2 formula.

options.text: Bromine donates two electrons to calcium
options.explanation: The halogen is the electron acceptor in these reactions.

options.text: Calcium is a Group 1 metal with one valence electron
options.explanation: Calcium is Group 2 and loses two electrons.

questions.stem: Iodine fails to oxidise iron(II) because

options.text: Iron(II) ions repel iodine molecules
options.explanation: No repulsion argument applies; the thermodynamics of electron capture decides.

options.text: Iron(II) is already fully oxidised
options.explanation: Iron(II) can still rise to iron(III), as chlorine and bromine prove.

options.text: Its electron capture is too weak to pull Fe2+ up to Fe3+
options.explanation: The oxidising power of iodine falls short of the iron(III)/iron(II) pull.

options.text: Iodine molecules cannot accept any electrons at all
options.explanation: Iodine accepts electrons from stronger reducing agents; it is just too weak for Fe2+.

questions.stem: In Cl2 + 2Fe2+ -> 2Cl- + 2Fe3+, how many electrons move in total?

options.text: Four, two per chlorine atom
options.explanation: Each chlorine atom gains only one electron to reach -1.

options.text: One, a single electron hops once
options.explanation: Two iron(II) ions are oxidised, so two electrons move.

options.text: None, this is not a redox reaction
options.explanation: Both iron and chlorine change oxidation number, so electrons transfer.

options.text: Two, one to each chlorine atom, one lost by each iron(II)
options.explanation: Each Fe2+ loses one electron and each chlorine atom gains one, so the ledger closes at two.

questions.stem: Mixing iron(III) solution with potassium iodide gives iodine because

options.text: Iron(III) is a strong enough oxidising agent to take electrons from iodide
options.explanation: Fe3+ oxidises I- to I2 while being reduced to Fe2+, the demonstrated reversal.

options.text: Iodine donates electrons to iron(III)
options.explanation: Iodide loses the electrons; iodine is the product of that oxidation.

options.text: Iron(III) reduces iodide to iodine
options.explanation: Reduction of iodide would keep it as I-, not produce I2.

options.text: The iodide acts as the oxidising agent
options.explanation: The oxidising agent is iron(III); iodide is oxidised.

questions.stem: Write the equation for calcium reacting with bromine.
questions.modelAnswer: Ca (s) + Br2 (l) -> CaBr2 (s), with calcium oxidised from 0 to +2.

questions.stem: State which halogens can oxidise iron(II) to iron(III).
questions.modelAnswer: Chlorine and bromine achieve the iron(III) oxidation; iodine cannot.

questions.stem: Explain why the halogens are described as oxidising agents in their reactions with metals.
questions.modelAnswer: In every such reaction the halogen molecules gain the electrons the metal atoms lose, so the halogen is reduced and the metal oxidised, which is precisely the action of an oxidising agent.

questions.stem: A solution of Fe2+ contaminated with I- is treated with chlorine water. State and explain the two redox changes that occur.
questions.modelAnswer: Chlorine oxidises both: each Fe2+ loses an electron to become Fe3+, and each I- loses an electron to give brown iodine, while the chlorine is reduced to chloride - two oxidations sharing one reduced reagent.

questions.stem: A disproportionation reaction is one in which

options.text: A compound splits into its elements
options.explanation: Decomposition into elements is not disproportionation.

options.text: A single species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced
options.explanation: Disproportionation splits one oxidation state into a higher and a lower one simultaneously.

options.text: Two different species exchange oxidation numbers
options.explanation: That is a normal redox reaction, not disproportionation.

options.text: A species is oxidised without any electron movement
options.explanation: Oxidation always involves electron loss or an equivalent oxidation-number rise.

questions.stem: In Cl2 + 2OH- -> Cl- + ClO- + H2O, the chlorine that becomes ClO- has been

options.text: Neither, because its charge is still negative
options.explanation: The ionic charge and oxidation number are different bookkeeping quantities.

options.text: Hydrated rather than redox-changed
options.explanation: The +1 oxidation state is a genuine redox change.

options.text: Oxidised, from 0 to +1
options.explanation: Rising to +1 in chlorate(I) means electron loss, so oxidation.

options.text: Reduced, from 0 to +1
options.explanation: A rise in oxidation number is oxidation, not reduction.

questions.stem: Which change happens to the chlorine that forms Cl- in cold alkali?

options.text: Oxidation, from 0 to -1
options.explanation: A falling oxidation number is reduction, not oxidation.

options.text: No change, since -1 is chlorine's usual state
options.explanation: The free chlorine started at 0, so the fall is a real change.

options.text: Displacement of hydroxide from solution
options.explanation: No displacement occurs; the chloride forms by electron gain.

options.text: Reduction, from 0 to -1 by gaining one electron
options.explanation: Falling to -1 is electron gain, the reduction branch of the disproportionation.

questions.stem: The cold-alkali ionic equation balances in charge because

options.text: The two hydroxide ions' -2 charge equals the chloride and chlorate(I) charges combined
options.explanation: -1 + (-1) = -2 on the right matches -2 on the left.

options.text: Water neutralises all charges on both sides
options.explanation: Water is neutral and cannot account for the charged balance.

options.text: Chlorine molecules carry no charge so charges vanish
options.explanation: The charged species on both sides must still balance.

options.text: Both sides sum to zero charge
options.explanation: Both sides carry -2, not zero.

questions.stem: Why does temperature matter for chlorine in alkali?

options.text: Hot alkali stops disproportionation entirely
options.explanation: Hot alkali still disproportionates, into the +5 branch.

options.text: Different temperatures give different products: cold alkali yields chlorate(I), hot alkali yields chlorate(V)
options.explanation: Around 15 degrees the +1 product forms; around 70 degrees the +5 product takes over.

options.text: Temperature changes only the rate, never the products
options.explanation: For chlorine in alkali the product identity itself changes with temperature.

options.text: Cold alkali prevents any reaction occurring
options.explanation: Cold alkali does react, giving the +1 branch.

questions.stem: Define disproportionation.
questions.modelAnswer: A reaction in which one species is simultaneously oxidised and reduced, splitting into a higher and a lower oxidation state.

questions.stem: Write the ionic equation for chlorine in cold dilute alkali.
Explain how the cold-alkali reaction shows disproportionation of chlorine.
questions.modelAnswer: One chlorine atom ends at -1 in chloride and another at +1 in chlorate(I), both from neutral chlorine at 0, so the same species has been reduced and oxidised in the same reaction.

questions.stem: A student claims chlorine in cold alkali is purely reduced because chloride forms. Correct the claim using oxidation numbers.
questions.modelAnswer: Only half the chlorine is reduced to -1; the other half rises to +1 in chlorate(I), so chlorine as a whole is disproportionated, oxidised and reduced simultaneously.

questions.stem: In hot alkali, chlorine's oxidation states after reaction are

options.text: -1 and +7, reaching perchlorate
options.explanation: Chlorate(VII) is not formed with dilute hot alkali here.

options.text: 0 throughout, as disproportionation needs no change
options.explanation: Disproportionation requires both a rise and a fall from 0.

options.text: -1 in chloride and +5 in chlorate(V)
options.explanation: Five atoms fall to -1 and one climbs to +5, the hot-alkali pair.

options.text: -1 and +1, as in the cold reaction
options.explanation: The +1 chlorate(I) belongs to cold alkali; heat switches the product to +5.

questions.stem: The electron ledger for 3Cl2 + 6OH- -> 5Cl- + ClO3- + 3H2O closes because

options.text: Each chlorine atom both gains and loses five electrons
options.explanation: Each atom takes exactly one branch, not both.

options.text: Hydroxide ions donate the missing five electrons
options.explanation: Hydroxide supplies oxygen and charge balance, not the redox electrons.

options.text: Water absorbs the extra electrons at the end
options.explanation: Water is a product, not an electron sink.

options.text: Five chlorine atoms each gain one electron while one chlorine atom loses five
options.explanation: 5 x 1 gained equals 1 x 5 lost, so the transfer is balanced.

questions.stem: Chlorate(V), ClO3-, contains chlorine with oxidation number

options.text: +5, since three oxygens at -2 plus +5 gives the -1 ion charge
+1, matching the cold-alkali product
options.explanation: That is chlorate(I), ClO-, a different ion.

options.text: +3, halfway between the branches
options.explanation: No chlorine(III) product appears in these equations.

options.text: -1, like all chlorine products
options.explanation: The chlorate(V) chlorine is oxidised, not reduced.

questions.stem: How many hydroxide ions appear in the hot-alkali ionic equation per 3 chlorine molecules?

options.text: Three, one per water formed
options.explanation: Three waters are formed but six hydroxides are consumed.

options.text: Six, supplying the oxygen atoms for chlorate(V) and the water
options.explanation: 6OH- provides the three oxygens of ClO3- and the three waters.

options.text: Two, exactly as in the cold-alkali equation
options.explanation: The cold equation's 2OH- does not carry enough oxygen for the hot products.

options.text: Five, one per chloride formed
options.explanation: Chloride needs no oxygen; the six hydroxides feed the oxide count.

questions.stem: Compared with the cold reaction, the hot reaction differs chiefly in

options.text: Whether disproportionation happens at all
options.explanation: Both temperatures give disproportionation; only the products differ.

options.text: The role of water as a product
options.explanation: Water forms in both ionic equations.

options.text: The oxidation state of the oxidised chlorine: +5 instead of +1
options.explanation: Heat shifts the disproportionation branch from chlorate(I) to chlorate(V).

options.text: The oxidation state of the reduced chlorine: -3 instead of -1
options.explanation: The reduced branch is still chloride at -1 in both.

questions.stem: Write the ionic equation for chlorine in hot dilute alkali.
State the oxidation-number changes chlorine undergoes in hot alkali.
questions.modelAnswer: Five atoms fall from 0 to -1 in chloride and one atom rises from 0 to +5 in chlorate(V).

questions.stem: Show that the hot-alkali equation is a disproportionation using electron counting.
questions.modelAnswer: Of the six chlorine atoms, five each gain one electron (0 to -1) and one loses five electrons (0 to +5); five gained equals five lost, so chlorine is both reduced and oxidised.

questions.stem: Predict, with reasoning, how many chlorate(V) ions form from 6 Cl2 molecules in excess hot alkali.
questions.modelAnswer: 6 Cl2 holds 12 chlorine atoms; one in six is oxidised, so 2 chlorate(V) ions form alongside 10 chloride ions, keeping the five-to-one ratio.

questions.stem: When chlorine reacts with water, the products are

options.text: Chloride and chlorate(V) ions only
options.explanation: That pair belongs to alkali conditions, not pure water.

options.text: Hydrogen and chlorine oxide gases
options.explanation: No gas evolution is the chemistry here; both products stay dissolved.

options.text: Sodium chloride and water
options.explanation: Sodium is not present in chlorine water.

options.text: Hydrochloric acid and chloric(I) acid
options.explanation: HCl and HClO form as chlorine is reduced and oxidised simultaneously.

questions.stem: The chlorine that ends in HClO has been

options.text: Oxidised from 0 to +1
options.explanation: Rising to +1 in the acid is the oxidation branch of the water disproportionation.

options.text: Reduced from 0 to +1
options.explanation: An oxidation-number rise is oxidation.

options.text: Unchanged, since HClO is neutral
options.explanation: Molecule neutrality does not fix the atom's oxidation number at 0.

options.text: Displaced from solution by the water
options.explanation: No displacement happens; chlorine reacts with the water itself.

questions.stem: Why does chloric(I) acid sterilise water?

options.text: It removes chlorine from the water again
options.explanation: The acid IS the chlorine treatment, not its removal.

options.text: It kills bacteria in the water
options.explanation: The +1 chlorine species is the bactericide that makes the supply safe.

options.text: It neutralises all dissolved salts
options.explanation: Sterilisation targets microbes, not salt content.

options.text: It raises the boiling point of the water
options.explanation: Boiling point is irrelevant to disinfection.

questions.stem: HClO dissociating in water gives

options.text: H2 and O2, decomposing to elements
options.explanation: No such decomposition occurs in solution.

options.text: HCl and hydroxide
options.explanation: That would reverse the disproportionation.

options.text: H+ and ClO-, and the chlorate(I) ion also sterilises
options.explanation: The dissociation spreads the +1 chlorine into a second active species.

options.text: H+ and Cl-, completing reduction
options.explanation: Cl- is the -1 branch, not the dissociation of HClO.

questions.stem: Which statement about chlorine in water is correct?

options.text: Chlorine only dissolves physically, without reaction
options.explanation: Chemical disproportionation occurs, not mere dissolution.

options.text: Only reduction of chlorine occurs in water
options.explanation: The +1 branch proves oxidation happens too.

options.text: The sterilising species is chloride ion
options.explanation: Chloride is the reduced, inactive branch; HClO and ClO- sterilise.

options.text: Chlorine is both oxidised and reduced, so the reaction is disproportionation
options.explanation: The 0 state splits into -1 (HCl) and +1 (HClO), the defining pattern.

questions.stem: Name the two acids formed when chlorine reacts with water.
State the role of ClO- in treated water.
questions.modelAnswer: The chlorate(I) ion acts as a sterilising agent, killing bacteria alongside chloric(I) acid.

questions.stem: Explain why treating water with chlorine is a disproportionation reaction.
questions.modelAnswer: Chlorine at 0 splits into the -1 state in HCl and the +1 state in HClO, so the same element is simultaneously reduced and oxidised.

questions.stem: A water board reduces chlorine dose but must still kill bacteria. Explain why a small dose can remain effective.
questions.modelAnswer: The +1 chlorine species are potent bactericides used catalytically in the sense that each HClO/ClO- unit attacks bacteria; even low concentrations maintain a sterilising presence throughout the supply.
